strengths: Addresses a genuine and impactful engineering problem (HLS design automation) with a well-motivated multi-agent LLM pipeline covering both error correction and design-space optimization, rather than tackling only one sub-problem.

The VODA data augmentation and bug-insertion pipeline is a reasonable systematic approach to overcoming the scarcity of labeled HLS error data, and the resulting dataset (12k+ buggy samples, 34 error types, preference pairs) is non-trivial engineering effort.

Empirical evaluation is broad: 612 debugging cases across three benchmark categories (Kernel/Vitis/Manual), comparison against multiple general LLM baselines (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama3.1-8B, DeepSeek-Coder) and prior domain-specific/DSL/learning-based methods (RALAD, Dahlia, HeteroCL, Allo, HGBO-DSE), with consistent improvements reported across metrics.
Ablation study (Figure 8) isolates contributions of the fine-tuned analysis agent, DPO alignment, and multi-attempt refinement, providing some insight into which architectural components matter.
weaknesses: Relevance to ACL/computational linguistics is weak: the paper's core contributions (HLS bug taxonomy, directive tuning, EDA tool integration, hardware QoR metrics) are domain-specific to hardware design automation, with LLM fine-tuning/agents used largely as an off-the-shelf tool rather than an NLP methodological contribution (no analysis of language understanding, prompting theory, or generalizable NLP techniques); this looks better suited to an EDA/hardware venue (DAC/ICCAD/FPGA) than ACL.

Reproducibility is limited: no clear statement of code/data/model release; the pipeline involves ~10 distinct LLM roles/agents, several proprietary or ad hoc prompt designs, and dataset construction procedures (bug insertion heuristics, CoT labeling) that are described only at a high level, making faithful reproduction difficult.

Evaluation lacks statistical rigor — no variance/error bars, no discussion of run-to-run stability of LLM outputs (LLMs are stochastic), and single-seed comparisons for speedup numbers (e.g., 14.8× peak) that could be sensitive to prompt/sample variance.

Baseline comparisons may be somewhat unfair: general-purpose LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude) are evaluated zero/few-shot without HLS-specific fine-tuning or the same multi-agent/iterative infrastructure that ChatHLS enjoys, which could inflate the apparent gap rather than isolating the true benefit of the proposed fine-tuning/data-augmentation method versus simply providing more agentic scaffolding to the baselines.

The proposed 'Energy Efficiency' metric (Eq. 2) is introduced ad hoc with an unexplained sigmoid/exponential parameterization and an unspecified sensitivity coefficient γ, undermining confidence in this evaluation metric's validity.

HLSTuner is only evaluated on five PolyBench kernels beyond the training set — a fairly narrow generalization test for claims of 'strong generalization potential' and large speedups (up to 14.8×) that are central to the paper's headline results.

The writing and figures are dense and, in places, garbled/duplicated in the extracted text (e.g., repeated figure captions), and architecture description (many interacting LLM agents labeled 1–10) is difficult to follow without a clearer schematic or algorithmic summary, hurting overall clarity.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated real-world bottleneck (HLS design correctness and optimization) and presents an end-to-end, engineering-complete pipeline (ChatHLS) combining error-correction and directive-optimization agents.

The evaluation is fairly extensive: 612 debugging test cases spanning 34 error types across three benchmark sources (Kernel/Vitis/Manual), and optimization results on PolyBench kernels compared against multiple categories of baselines (general LLMs, RAG-based RALAD, DSL-based Dahlia/HeteroCL/Allo, learning-based HGBO-DSE).

An ablation study for HLSFixer (fixing-only vs. +analysis vs. +DPO vs. full multi-agent iteration) isolates the contribution of individual design choices, which supports internal validity of the debugging component's claims.

Reasonable reproducibility details are given for the fine-tuning setup (Llama3-8B, LoRA, optimizer, learning rate schedule, epoch counts, hardware), and the paper documents distinct error taxonomies (Table 1) that could aid replication of the general approach.
weaknesses: Relevance to computational linguistics/NLP is weak: the paper is fundamentally an EDA/hardware-design-automation contribution that uses off-the-shelf SFT+DPO fine-tuning and a multi-agent LLM pipeline as a tool; there is no NLP-specific methodological novelty, linguistic analysis, or contribution to core language-model research that would be of primary interest to an ACL audience versus a hardware/CAD venue (DAC/ICCAD/ASP-DAC).

No statement about releasing code, datasets (12,352 buggy samples, 3,489 preference pairs, 4,804 optimization samples), trained model checkpoints, or the exact multi-agent prompts/pipeline configuration; given the system's complexity (10 distinct LLM roles, BugRAG, iterative refinement loops), independent reproduction from the paper's description alone would be very difficult without released artifacts.

Results are reported as single-point estimates (pass rates, speedups) with no variance, confidence intervals, or repeated-run statistics, making it hard to assess robustness of headline numbers (e.g., 82.7% pass rate, 14.8x peak speedup) or whether differences over baselines are statistically meaningful.

The optimization evaluation (HLSTuner) is conducted on only five PolyBench kernels, a very small and somewhat narrow benchmark set for claims of strong generalization; it is unclear how representative these kernels are of realistic, larger-scale HLS workloads, and whether the reported speedups would hold at larger design sizes.

Baseline comparisons (e.g., against GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, RALAD) do not specify whether these models were given equivalent prompting effort, iteration budgets, or in-context examples, raising concerns about a level playing field; the paper states general LLMs get up to five attempts while HLSTuner is one-shot, but it is unclear if this asymmetry is fair or simply reflects the fine-tuned model having absorbed benchmark-adjacent priors.

The energy-efficiency metric (Eq. 2) is a custom, ad hoc proxy with hand-chosen functional forms and a free sensitivity coefficient γ, whose validity as a proportional stand-in for real chip-level energy is not justified or validated against actual power measurements.

It is unclear whether the test kernels/benchmarks used for evaluation (Vitis examples, manually crafted designs, PolyBench kernels) have any overlap with the sources used to construct the BugRAG error taxonomy or training data, beyond the claim that 'experiments were excluded from the training distribution,' which is asserted rather than demonstrated (e.g., no held-out kernel/error-type split description).

strengths: Comprehensive, well-engineered multi-agent system (ChatHLS) that decomposes the HLS-C generation, debugging, and directive-tuning problem into specialized sub-tasks (HLSTuner, HLSFixer, VODA/BugRAG), each with a clear training strategy (SFT, DPO, CoT distillation from a teacher model).

Extensive empirical evaluation against a wide range of baselines: general-purpose LLMs (DeepSeek-V3.2, Gemini-3-pro, Claude-opus-4.5), RAG-augmented variants, prior LLM-for-HLS work (RALAD/HLSRewriter/C2HLSC), DSL-based tools (Dahlia, HeteroCL, Allo), and learning-based DSE (HGBO-DSE).

Careful ablations isolating the contribution of retrieval vs. specialized fine-tuning (Appendix E), model-scale scaling analysis, token-cost analysis, and train/test similarity checks (Rouge-L) to reduce leakage concerns.
Post-implementation (place-and-route) validation demonstrating that reported latency improvements are physically realizable rather than artifacts of infeasible directive insertion.
Detailed error taxonomy (33 HLS-specific error types) and dataset construction pipeline (BugRAG, controlled bug injection) that could be a useful resource if released.
Clear documentation of experimental settings, training hyperparameters, and benchmark composition in the appendix, aiding reproducibility to some extent.
weaknesses: Relevance to computational linguistics/NLP is weak: the paper is fundamentally an EDA/hardware-design-automation contribution that uses LLMs as a tool (via standard SFT/DPO/CoT-distillation/RAG recipes) rather than advancing NLP methodology, understanding, or evaluation; ACL's stated relevance criterion is not clearly met beyond "LLM applications."

The core technical machinery (multi-agent pipelines, CoT distillation from a teacher model, DPO with CoT/non-CoT pairs, RAG with a bug repository) is largely a combination of existing, well-established techniques from the software-engineering/agent literature, applied to a new domain; the paper does not clearly articulate what is methodologically novel from an NLP/ML standpoint.

Reproducibility is constrained by reliance on closed, versioned proprietary models (DeepSeek-V3.2 as teacher/judge, Gemini-3-pro, Claude-opus-4.5, GPT-5/5.1) whose behavior may drift or be inaccessible to future researchers, and by proprietary/commercial HLS toolchains (Vitis HLS) needed to reproduce QoR results.

Potential evaluation circularity: some judgments (e.g., ablation comparisons, multi-agent scoring) use LLMs from the same families being compared against (e.g., Gemini-3-Pro as judge), which could bias reported gains.

Baselines for optimization speedup (Vitis HLS auto-pipeline) are relatively weak, and very large reported speedups (e.g., 60x+) partly reflect baseline failures/penalization schemes (e.g., assigning speedup=1 when baselines fail 15/15 trials) rather than uniformly strong comparisons; no human-expert-designed baseline is included for either debugging or optimization tasks.

Dataset and CoT supervision are generated entirely by a single teacher LLM (DeepSeek-V3.2), raising concerns about systematic biases or blind spots being propagated into the fine-tuned models, and no analysis of error/failure modes introduced by this teacher-generated supervision is provided.

The paper's dense multi-agent architecture (10 distinct LLM roles) makes the system difficult to follow and reduces analyzability of which components are actually responsible for the reported gains beyond the coarse ablation in Figure 7.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmark suites (PolyBench, MachSuite, CHStone, Rosetta, plus real accelerators like MobileNet and Transformer), providing broad coverage of both HLS-C generation and directive-tuning tasks.

Careful ablation studies isolating the contribution of each component (fixing-only vs. analysis agent vs. DPO vs. multi-LLM judge), which helps substantiate the claimed gains rather than presenting only aggregate numbers.

Thoughtful control experiments addressing an obvious confound: the matched-RAG baselines (Appendix E) directly test whether simple retrieval augmentation alone could close the gap to the proposed system, strengthening the causal claim that specialized data curation and fine-tuning (not just domain documents) drive improvement.

Rouge-L train/test similarity analysis to mitigate data leakage concerns, and post-implementation (place-and-route) validation showing reported latency gains are physically realizable rather than synthesis artifacts.
Reasonably detailed error taxonomy (33 HLS-specific error types) and transparent reporting of limitations (lack of DATAFLOW/AXI directive support, single FPGA platform validation).
weaknesses: Relevance to ACL/computational linguistics is questionable: the core contribution is an EDA/hardware-design application. While it uses SFT, DPO, RAG, and LLM-as-judge, none of these techniques are advanced or studied at a methodological level for NLP researchers—the paper is primarily an application paper for a hardware-design audience, which may sit outside typical ACL scope despite the LLM-centric framing.

Potential circularity in data/evaluation: all training data (CoT, buggy code, optimization strategies) is generated by DeepSeek-V3.2 as the teacher model, and DeepSeek-V3.2 is also used as one of the main baselines being compared against and as the insertion/code-modification agent within ChatHLS itself; this blending of teacher and baseline roles complicates a clean attribution of gains to the proposed framework versus the underlying model family.

Some headline numbers (e.g., "32.6% relative improvement," "41.8% generation success rate improvement," "3.3× speedup") are drawn from different metrics/sections and could be seen as selectively highlighted; the paper would benefit from a single, clearly defined primary metric per contribution to avoid the impression of cherry-picked framing.

The multi-agent architecture (10 distinct LLM instances/roles) is described at a high level, but it remains unclear which agents are separately fine-tuned checkpoints versus prompted instances of the same backbone, and what the end-to-end computational/latency cost of orchestrating 10 agents is in practice—this limits reproducibility and understanding of the true system complexity.

Benchmark scale for HLS-C generation (108 tasks) and debugging (591 cases, derived from only 32 base designs via synthetic error injection) is relatively modest, and many test kernels are classic textbook benchmarks (PolyBench/MachSuite) rather than large, realistic industrial designs, limiting external validity claims despite the MobileNet/Transformer case studies.

Reproduced baselines (e.g., RALAD with GPT-5.1) may not fully replicate the original method's intended configuration, and the paper does not report variance/confidence intervals for many pass@k and speedup numbers despite using stochastic LLM sampling (temperature=0.7 in several settings).
